note: Pierce crystal oscillators for microcontrollers: load capacitance, gain margin, drive level, layout and grounding. Extracted 2026-10-27; quotes checked by tools/library_quotes.py. ST AN2867 was read at Rev 10 from a mirror (st.com unreachable; current is Rev 24): re-check its wording.

claims.statement: Choose the two load capacitors so that C1*C2/(C1+C2) plus the stray capacitance (pins + PCB) equals the crystal's specified CL; with C1 = C2 this gives C1 = C2 = 2*(CL - Cs).

citations.quote: if the CL value of the crystal is equal to 15 pF and, assuming that Cs = 5 pF
citations.figure: Worked example: CL - Cs = CL1 x CL2 / (CL1 + CL2) = 10 pF, that is CL1 = CL2 = 20 pF.

citations.quote: The product design engineer selects the values of capacitors C2 and C3 to match the crystal CL
The total CL consists of the loading capacitors and the parasitic capacitance of the layout and packaging.
the series combination is 7.5 pF ... total load capacitance of 10.5pF, which is close enough to the target of 10 pF.

claims.could_enforce: schematic check: given crystal CL and a stray budget, verify C1, C2 values (package check already pins RP2350 values)
claims.note: Values are first estimates; ST §4.2 step 2 says to fine-tune experimentally against a characterised crystal.

claims.statement: Budget 2-5 pF of stray capacitance (oscillator pins plus PCB traces) in the load-capacitance calculation, and keep XIN/XOUT traces short so it stays inside that budget.

citations.quote: Stray capacitance can be assumed to be in the range of 2 to 5 pF ... minimized by keeping traces as short as possible.
The load capacitance calculation should also include the board capacitance (about 2-3 pF) and the driver's capacitance
Parasitic capacitance will reduce gain margin ... XTALIN to ground: 1pF, XTALOUT to ground: 2pF, XTALIN to XTALOUT: 0.5pF
stray capacitance is the addition of the microcontroller pin capacitance (OSC_IN and OSC_OUT) and the PCB capacitance
We'll assume a value of 3 pF for this ... we therefore need to keep them small so we don't upset the crystal

enforced_by: intent max_length on XIN, XOUT (rp2350 package)
claims.could_enforce: extract XIN/XOUT net capacitance from geometry (trace area over reference plane + pad) and compare with the stray budget used for the load caps

claims.statement: Load capacitors are C0G/NP0 (low leakage, stable over temperature).

citations.quote: Load capacitors should be low leakage and stable across temperature (NPO or COG type)
Select capacitors with a low temperature coefficient such as NP0 or C0G types.

claims.could_enforce: part check: dielectric field of load capacitors

claims.statement: Oscillator gain margin gm/gmcrit is at least 5, where gmcrit = 4*(ESR + Rext)*(2*pi*F)^2*(C0 + CL)^2 using the crystal's maximum ESR; if it is not, pick a crystal with lower ESR or lower CL.

citations.quote: highly recommended that the selected crystal has a gain margin higher than or equal to 5. Try to select a crystal with a lower ESR
the value of RExt has to be added to ESR in the expression of gm >> gmcrit

claims.could_enforce: schematic check needing MCU gm (from datasheet) and crystal ESR, C0, CL; the RP2350 datasheet would have to supply gm
claims.note: Example in ST: 8 MHz, C0 7 pF, CL 10 pF, ESR 80 ohm gives gmcrit 0.23 mA/V.

claims.statement: Measured oscillator negative resistance (smallest series resistor that stops start-up) is at least 5x the crystal ESR for MHz oscillators; 3x is the floor accepted for 32 kHz/industrial use.

citations.quote: for the LSE oscillator, the oscillation is considered safe for a safety factor higher than or equal to x3, while for the HSE ... x5.
Typically, most industrial applications seek a factor of 3, while automotive applications seek a factor of at least 5.
on par with some other reputable crystal manufacturers' guidelines to have a GhO of 5 to account for temperature and worst case part deviations.

claims.could_enforce: bench test record attached to the package (not a layout check); layout can keep a footprint position for the test resistor
claims.note: This is a test of the built board, not a geometric rule. ST defines Sf = (R_ADD + ESR)/ESR; AN949 compares R3 alone with ESR.

claims.statement: For TI CC13xx/CC26xx/CC23xx/CC27xx, negative-resistance magnitude is at least 10x ESR at initial start-up and at least 5x in steady state (automotive).

citations.quote: TI recommends that the magnitude of the negative resistance be at least 10 times greater than the ESR during the initial start-up

claims.note: Stricter than ST/Microchip; TI accepts 3x only with its software amplitude compensation.

claims.statement: Lower CL (smaller load capacitors) raises negative resistance and shortens start-up but makes frequency more sensitive to board capacitance; larger load capacitors improve stability but cut loop gain.

citations.quote: Equation 7 approximates the negative resistance and shows that a low CL gives a larger negative resistance.
Frequency becomes more sensitive to changes in board capacitance as CL decreases.
Large values increase frequency stability but decrease the loop gain and may cause oscillator start-up problems.
Generally speaking, the higher the load capacitance (CL) of a crystal, the lower its pullability.

claims.could_enforce: generator scoring of crystal choice, not layout

claims.statement: Drive level in the crystal, DL = 2*ESR*(pi*F*(CL+C0)*Vpp)^2, does not exceed the crystal's rated maximum (200 uW for the ABM8-272-T3); overdrive ages, shifts or fractures the crystal.

citations.quote: Exceeding this value can damage or reduce the life of the crystal. Equation 5 gives the drive level in W.
Exceeding this maximum value may lead to the crystal being damaged or to a shorter device lifetime.
Overdriving the crystal can cause excessive aging, frequency shift, and/or quartz fracture and eventual failure.

citations.figure: Key electrical specifications table: Drive Level, 10 uW typical, 200 uW maximum.

claims.could_enforce: bench measurement (Vpp at XIN with <1 pF probe) recorded against the package; not geometric

claims.statement: When the crystal would be overdriven, a series resistor sits between XOUT and the crystal, starting at the reactance of the XOUT-side load capacitor, Rext = 1/(2*pi*F*C2); with C2 it also low-passes overtones.

citations.quote: voltage divider formed by RExt/CL2. Thus, the value of RExt is equal to the reactance of CL2.
With CL2, it forms a low-pass filter that forces the oscillator to start at the fundamental frequency
a 1 kΩ series resistor (R2), is a good value to prevent the crystal being over-driven ... IOVDD level of 3.3 V.

enforced_by: ccomp check package (part values) for RP2350
claims.note: For RP2350 (12 MHz, 15 pF) the ST estimate is 884 ohm; Raspberry Pi's tested 1 kohm is consistent. Rext must be added to ESR in the gain-margin check, and lower IOVDD needs a smaller Rext (rp2350_hdg).

claims.statement: A 32.768 kHz oscillator has no external series resistor; Rext is fitted only when the measured drive level exceeds the crystal rating, otherwise it is 0 ohm.

citations.quote: In the 32 kHz oscillator part, however, it is not recommended to use an external resistor.
the insertion of RExt is not recommended and its value is then 0 Ω.

claims.statement: A 32 kHz tuning-fork oscillator gets a series resistor between oscillator output and crystal (with a footprint always provided) to suppress the ~200 kHz spurious torsional mode and limit start-up current.

citations.quote: put in series with the crystal a resistor that creates an additional phase lag with crystal capacitor C2
The best strategy is to implement the footprint on the PCB for the resistor and capacitor C3.

claims.note: TI note is for the TPS65950 32 kHz cell and says it may not generalise; still a direct disagreement with ST's general advice.

claims.statement: Crystal, load capacitors and damping resistor sit as close as possible to the MCU oscillator pins, on the same side of the board, so XIN/XOUT traces are short.

citations.quote: The crystal should be mounted as close as possible to the microcontroller to keep short tracks and to reduce inductive and capacitive effects.
the oscillator circuit should be placed next to the controller and on the same surface.
Place the crystal as close as possible to the device to minimize the length of the PCB traces.
The best practice is to place the crystal and phasing capacitors as close as possible to the TPS65950 part.
Try and keep the layout as short as possible.

enforced_by: intent max_length on XIN, XOUT (rp2350 package)
claims.could_enforce: part_distance_mm from crystal/caps to MCU pins; same-side check

claims.statement: The XIN load capacitor is placed first and closest to the XIN pin and its ground, and the two load capacitors sit close to each other.

citations.quote: The load XTALIN capacitor should be placed first and closest to the XTALIN pin and ground
The load capacitors should be placed close to each other

claims.could_enforce: placement_order: XIN cap before crystal on the XIN net; part_distance_mm between the two load caps

claims.statement: The two load-capacitor branches are laid out symmetrically, with ground connections of identical length.

citations.quote: Symmetry between oscillator capacitances
The connections must be as short as possible and of identical lengths.

claims.could_enforce: length_match between XIN-cap and XOUT-cap ground connections

claims.statement: No high-frequency, clock or fast-switching traces run near or through the crystal area, on its layer or the adjacent layer; both XIN and XOUT are victims.

citations.quote: Keep other digital signal lines, especially clock lines and frequently switching signal lines, as far away from the crystal connections as possible.
Any path conveying high-frequency signals should be routed away from the oscillator paths and components.
do not route signal traces through the crystal area. Both oscillator pin connections are critical.
Make sure no high-speed digital signals are close to the crystal to minimize cross-coupling of noise into the oscillator.

claims.could_enforce: region keep-out around crystal block (all layers above the reference plane) for foreign nets, plus clearance_mm from aggressor nets to XIN/XOUT
claims.note: No source gives a number; the distance would need simulation or an expert value.

claims.statement: If the crystal cannot sit at the pins, XIN/XOUT do not run long distances under the MCU package or form loops.

citations.quote: all connections must be routed carefully to avoid passing under the package with long traces or making critical loops

claims.could_enforce: length of XIN/XOUT inside the MCU courtyard

claims.statement: XIN and XOUT traces are routed apart to minimise the XIN-XOUT parasitic capacitance (typically 0.5 pF).

citations.quote: Reduce the parasitic capacitance between XTALIN and XTALOUT pins by routing them as far apart as possible

claims.could_enforce: clearance_mm between XIN and XOUT nets (beyond the pin pitch)

claims.statement: XIN/XOUT carry no test points or stubs beyond the crystal, load caps and damping resistor.

citations.quote: Too many test points.

claims.could_enforce: count of pads on XIN/XOUT nets other than MCU pin, crystal, caps, resistor
claims.note: ST lists this as a flaw in a failing example, not a stated rule; weak evidence.

claims.statement: The two load capacitors' grounds join each other close to the crystal and return by a short direct path to the MCU's oscillator ground, away from the return currents of USB, PWM, power and other noisy circuits.

citations.quote: the best practice is to connect close to the crystal, the two capacitors before connecting to the ground reference.
the loading capacitor grounds should be connected directly back to the controller ... The exception would be if a ground plane is present
The ground connection for the load capacitors should be short and avoid the return currents from USB, RS232, LIN, PWM,… and power lines

claims.could_enforce: decoupling_path_mm-style measure: cap ground pad to MCU ground pin; overlap with known high-current return regions

claims.statement: The crystal sits over the solid board ground plane; a separate ground island under the oscillator tied to main ground at one point is worse.

citations.quote: TI recommends a solid ground plane under the crystal.
Putting a separate ground under the crystal and the oscillator connected to the reference ground plane generally causes a worse situation.
A separate plane connected by one point can behave like an antenna.

citations.measured: board-wide GND fill on B.Cu covers the crystal centre and all four corner points; no separate island (2-layer board).

claims.could_enforce: unreferenced_length_mm of XIN/XOUT = 0 and crystal footprint fully over the main GND zone on the adjacent layer

claims.statement: The oscillator gets a dedicated local ground plane underneath, distinct from the application ground plane and connected to the nearest MCU ground pin.

citations.quote: The oscillator PCB should be underlined with a dedicated underneath ground plane, distinct from the application PCB ground plane.
The oscillator ground plane should be connected to the nearest microcontroller ground.
A ground area should be placed under the crystal oscillator area. This ground land should be connected to the oscillator ground.

claims.note: AVR186 Figure 1-1 labels a 'Local Ground plane' with a single 'Ground Plane Connection'. Both camps agree there is ground under the crystal; they disagree on whether it is the main plane or an island. A candidate for the slow-tier experiment.

claims.statement: A ground guard ring, connected to the ground plane, surrounds the crystal, load capacitors and XIN/XOUT traces.

citations.quote: A guard ring around these connections, connected to the ground, is essential to avoid capturing unwanted noise
Guard ring connected to the GND plane around the oscillator
only one PCB layer, it is recommended to place a guard ring around the oscillator components and to connect it to the oscillator ground pin
A guard ring, ground plane or shielding around the oscillator circuit may also be helpful.

claims.could_enforce: presence of a GND copper ring enclosing the crystal block on the component layer, stitched to the plane
claims.note: Sources differ in strength: ST calls it essential; AVR186 asks for it only on single-layer boards; TI SWRA495/SWCA076 do not mention one. All that mention a ring ground it; none recommends a floating ring. The RP2350 guide is silent.

claims.statement: The crystal's ground/case pads (pins 2 and 4 on 4-pad 3225 parts) connect to ground.

citations.quote: Connect the external capacitors needed for the crystal and the ceramic resonator operation as well as the crystal housing to the ground plane

citations.locator: Page (4) of (9), Mechanical Dimensions, top view
citations.figure: Top view labels pins 4 and 2 'GND' (figure label).

citations.measured: pad 2 GND, pad 4 GND, pad 1 /XIN, pad 3 to C4/R2.

claims.could_enforce: net check: crystal case pads on GND

claims.statement: A crystal in a metal package is not connected to the oscillator ground.

citations.quote: Note that if a crystal in a metallic package is used, it should not been connected to the oscillator ground.

claims.note: Ambiguous: ST may mean the dedicated oscillator ground island (crystal.ground.local_plane) rather than ground in general, i.e. tie the case to the main plane instead. Could not check whether ST's Rev 24 rewords this.

claims.statement: Frequency error budget = crystal tolerance + (load-capacitance deviation from cap tolerance and PCB stray variation) x pullability, with pullability = Cm*1e6/(2*(C0+CL)^2) ppm/pF.

citations.quote: Deviation (CL) ... measures the deviation of the load capacitance (CL) due to tolerances on load capacitor values and the variation of the stray capacitance
Any change on the capacitances listed above directly shifts the oscillation frequency.

claims.could_enforce: schematic check for USB/RF clocks against an allowed ppm limit
claims.note: Temperature drift is excluded from this budget (ST note p.25).
